rows: Cats see about a fifth to a tenth as much detail as people do. This view is blurred to match.
Cats have two kinds of colour-sensing cells in their eyes, where people have three. Reds and greens are hard for them to tell apart, so reds look olive or grey to a cat.
A cat’s pupil closes to a narrow vertical slit, a shape common in animals that hunt by ambush. A slit like this smears out-of-focus things up and down, and this view does the same.
A cat takes in about 200 degrees around itself, and a person about 180. A phone camera sees far less than either, so this view bends the picture at its edges to suggest the wider sweep.
Cats can see in light six to eight times dimmer than people need. This view brightens the shadows to show it.
A phone camera can’t measure distance, so this view assumes that things lower in the picture are closer. Tap the screen to move the focus.
This view assumes that a cat sees most sharply straight ahead.

rows: If you are a domestic cat, a chart test gave one gray tabby about 8 cycles per degree and a younger cat about 18, where a human reads about 30. Behavior studies put cats between 3 and 9.

If you are a domestic cat, you have two kinds of cone, one most sensitive near 450 nanometers in the blue and one near 556 in the yellow-green, where a human has three. Reds and oranges lose their color for you.
In bright light your pupil shrinks to an upright slit, as the pupils of your felid ancestors did. Lions and other large cats keep a round one.
Behind your retina, in the upper back of the eye, lies a mirror-like layer of cells called a tapetum cellulosum. The pigment cells over it carry no dark granules.
If you are a domestic cat, your sharpest sight lies in a cone-rich patch called the area centralis. You have no macula like a human's.
If you are a domestic cat, each degree of a quick eye jump adds about 3 milliseconds to its length. Peak eye speed climbs about 13.6 degrees per second for every degree of jump.

Nobody has measured how fast sharpness fades from your area centralis toward the edge of your sight, or how vivid your two-cone colors are beside a human's. Studies report cats six times as sensitive to light as humans in dim light, but the exact lift and the strength of your eye shine remain guesses.
Nobody has measured some parts of how you see, so they are guesses.
Cats have two kinds of colour-sensing cells in their eyes, where people have three. Reds and greens are hard for them to tell apart, so reds look olive or gray to a cat.
A cat takes in about 200 degrees around itself, and a person about 180. A phone camera sees far less than either, so this view bends the picture at its edges to suggest the wider sweep.
Cats can see in light six to eight times dimmer than people need. This view brightens the shadows to show it.
A phone camera can’t measure distance, so this view assumes that things lower in the picture are closer. Tap the screen to move the focus.
This view assumes that a cat sees most sharply straight ahead.
On this trial the colours come from the measured receptor peaks (450, 550 nm). The camera's colours and the display are the app's.
As the light falls, the colours drift toward what the rods take in, which peak near 501 nm. The peak is measured; where the change happens is the app's guess.

A cat sees in dim light partly by pooling light over time. With &draw=exposure, in the dark the picture pools the last few seconds, so still things settle and moving things leave ghosts. The pooling time is the app's.

windowS.note: seconds of pooling in the dark; the pooling time is the app's (atlas 7)

rows.title: Sharpness
rows.text: If you are a domestic cat, you read about 10 cycles a degree, a third of the 30 that a human reads on an eye chart. If you are a cheetah, you read about 25. If you are a wildcat of the same genus as the domestic cat, such as a sand cat, you very likely see about as sharply as it does, but for the other cats nobody has measured how sharply you see.
rows.note: Cheetah figure rounded from 23 to 25. Left out R3 (qualitative only) and R4 (Lynx lynx estimate with no stated method).

rows.title: Color
rows.text: If you are a domestic cat, you have two kinds of color-sensing cell, where a human has three. One kind senses blue light most strongly and the other senses yellow-green light most strongly. Blue-sensing cells have also been found in the cheetah, the bobcat and the leopard, and nobody has measured how many kinds of color-sensing cell other cats have.

cites.taxon: Acinonyx jubatus, Lynx rufus, Panthera pardus

rows.note: R3 is a dog measurement (429 nm), so I did not use it for any cat; the row gives no peak figures.

rows.title: Pupil
rows.text: If you are a domestic cat, an African wildcat, an ocelot, a serval or a fishing cat, the pupil in the middle of each eye is a vertical slit. If you are a lion, tiger, leopard, jaguar, mountain lion or cheetah, your pupil is round. If you are a bobcat, a caracal, a Canada lynx or an Iberian lynx, it is nearly round, and if you are a Eurasian lynx, it is oval to diamond-shaped.
rows.note: Species with grade g or i are not named; the row names only species with a measured pupil record. No record gives a reason for the shapes, so none is stated.

rows.title: Field of view
rows.text: If you are a domestic cat, each of your eyes sees from straight out on its own side to 30 degrees past your nose on the other side. Wildcats, the jungle cat and the other cats of the genus Felis are relatives of the domestic cat, and you very likely have the same field if you are one of them. Nobody has measured the field of view in a lynx, a lion or any other cat outside that genus.
rows.note: Left out R2 (140 degrees binocular): it does not fit R1's 30 degrees across the midline, which would give only about 60 degrees of overlap. Needs a check before use.

rows.title: Dim light
rows.text: If you are a domestic cat, the tapetum, a mirror-like layer at the back of your eye, reflects up to 130 times more light than the back of a human eye does, and you can detect light up to 7 times dimmer than a human can. Lions have a tapetum too, a milky blue one. Nobody has measured how faint a light a lion or most other cats can see.
rows.note: Figures are from domestic cat only; the tapetum is recorded in lion but no dim-light threshold exists for other species.

rows.title: Depth
rows.text: If you are a domestic cat, what your two eyes see overlaps across about 140 degrees, the same as in a human, and you probably cannot focus on anything closer than about 25 centimeters. Nobody has measured the overlap or the closest focus in most other cats, including lions, lynxes and bobcats.
rows.note: Left out R3 (blur of horizontal contours with a slit pupil): the quote does not state a depth cue or that every cat has a vertical slit.

rows.title: Sharpest spot
rows.text: If you are a domestic cat, you see most sharply in a small area toward the temple side of your retina, where one kind of color-sensing cell is packed densest. If you are a cheetah, that kind of cell forms a horizontal streak across your retina, as it does in other animals of open ground. Nobody has measured the sharpest spot in most other cats.
rows.note: Left out the Spanish wildcat (R1): its cone density figure is a comparison with the domestic cat and had no job here.
